newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Clinton classmate eyes Philippine presidency.
newsitem.headline: Clinton classmate eyes Philippine presidency.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton could find himself face-to-face with a former classmate at any summit between the United States and the Philippines after mid-1998.

Philippine Senator Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo, who studied with Clinton at Washington's Georgetown University in the 1960s, plans to succeed president Fidel Ramos and become the country's second woman president at the May 1998 elections.
A dimunitive 49-year-old with a doctorate in economics, Macapagal-Arroyo is currently riding high in opinion polls in the Philippines.
"My popularity, my acceptance by the people, my satisfaction rate has just been going up all the time," she told Reuters in an interview on Friday at her sprawling villa in Manila.
"In fact, I'm either leading at the surveys now or I am tying or I'm a close second. But anyway from a non-entity a year ago to a leading contender now, that's what I am."
But Macapagal-Arroyo said she is still to take "the formal, irrevocable decision" to run for president, although there appears little doubt she will do so.
Under Philippine law, people can only formally declare their candidacy three months before an election, when campaigning starts.

A daughter of former president Diosdado Macapagal, she was the head of the economics department at a local college when she was appointed by then-President Corazon Aquino, the nation's first female leader, to a government post in 1986.

In 1992, she won a seat in the Senate for Aquino's Laban party, currently the main opposition. She repeated the feat in 1995, with the highest number of votes ever won by a Philippine senator -- over 16 million.
But some weeks ago she left Laban to form her own party, amid reports that Laban was not prepared to endorse her candidacy for the presidency.

"In the past few months, we got the feeling that the Laban that Ninoy (Corazon Aquino's late husband) formed is no longer the Laban that we see today. There has been a trend toward autocratic rule rather than democratic rule. Those who were supporting me for president were ousted without even a hearing," she said.

Now, she says, she plans to build on her image as one of the prime movers of the economic reforms which, in recent years, have transformed the Philippines from a debt-ridden nation to one of the fastest-growing democracies in Asia.

"President Ramos speaks of 60 laws that brought about our economic restructuring," she said. "I authored 37 of them. Perhaps that's one reason why I got so many votes in the last elections and one reason why people now look upon me as somebody who can lead the country."
Macapagal-Arroyo said she would continue the reforms and bring about more social justice to alleviate poverty. She said she would be especially tough on corruption in public life.

"In the next century, I hope to see that we have been able to meet the centuries-old problem of mass poverty in the Philippines," she said. "We want to be prospersous, world-competitive. But in the face of all that, (we want to be a nation) that cares about the sustainability of the environment, the care of the young and the nourishment of the vulnerable."

She is confident that she can defeat Vice-President Joseph Estrada, a former matinee idol who has run neck and neck with Macapagal-Arroyo in the popularity surveys. Estrada has said it is his destiny to be the next president and is forecast as the leading candidate at the polls.
Ramos is barred by the country's constitution from seeking another term.
President Clinton is a close friend, Macapagal-Arroyo said, and the two meet whenever they are in each other's countries.

"We were in the same class and were as close as classmates can be," she said. "I was 17 and he was 18 ... both coming from hometowns very far away from the big city. He and I were both on the dean's list."
And their friendship, she said, would certainly help the United States and the Philippines, a former U.S. colony, to go hand-in-hand into the next century.
